title: Three days of worsening breathlessness in a 67-year-old man with heart failure
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 67-year-old man with known heart failure and atrial fibrillation who comes to the ED with 3 days of worsening exertional breathlessness, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea and ankle swelling. The candidate then interprets his observations, ECG, bloods and chest X-ray. They diagnose acute decompensated heart failure, identify a recent course of over-the-counter ibuprofen as the likely precipitant (with an acute kidney injury), weigh the differentials, outline ED management and safety-net for discharge.
focus: Worsening breathlessness in known heart failure: eliciting congestion and the precipitants of decompensation, reading the chest X-ray and bloods, and managing acute decompensated heart failure in the ED
context: Known heart failure and atrial fibrillation
stem: You are a final-year medical student on your Emergency Department placement at a metropolitan hospital. It is early afternoon. Bernard Hughes, a 67-year-old man, has come in because he is more short of breath. He is in an acute bay on a cardiac monitor with an IV cannula in place. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. The nurse has taken his observations and recorded an ECG, bloods have been sent and a chest X-ray has been requested. The ED registrar has asked you to see him first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Bernard and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, ECG, blood results and chest X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Bernard Hughes, a 67-year-old retired bank manager. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You are sitting propped up on the trolley at about 45 degrees. You are breathless but can speak in sentences, pausing now and then for breath. You are calm and cooperative, a little worried. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Bernard came in about 20 minutes ago. At triage his resp rate was 24, sats 91% on room air, heart rate 104 and irregular, BP 146/88, temp 36.8. The repeat just now was resp rate 26, sats 91%, heart rate 108, BP 144/86. He's on the monitor, the cannula's in, bloods have gone, the ECG is done and the X-ray has been requested."

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they ask for oxygen, the nurse asks, "What saturation are you aiming for?" On nasal prongs your sats come up to about 95% and you feel a little easier.
  • If they try to lie you flat, for example to examine you, say: "I can't lie flat, I'll be gasping." If they lie you flat anyway, you become more breathless and the nurse says your sats have dropped to 90%. Sitting you back up settles it.
  • If they ask for IV furosemide, the nurse asks what dose and gives it. Nothing changes within the station time, but you ask for a urine bottle.
  • If the candidate asks to check his doses (pharmacy, My Health Record, or phoning his wife), the nurse reads out: furosemide 40 mg each morning, candesartan 16 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 47.5 mg daily, rivaroxaban 20 mg daily, allopurinol 300 mg daily, rosuvastatin 10 mg daily.
  • If they call the ED registrar, the nurse says: "They're on their way, keep going."
  • If they explain what they are doing, you are reassured. If they use jargon, ask what it means.
  • If they ask for results now, the examiner says these will be given in Part 2.

Opening line: "I just can't get my breath like I used to. It's been getting worse these last few days."

History (give only when asked):

The breathlessness

  • Onset: you noticed 3 days ago that you were more short of breath. It came on gradually and has slowly got worse since. It did not come on suddenly.
  • Exercise tolerance: before this you walked a couple of kilometres every day without any trouble. Now you struggle to walk down the block.
  • Now: a bit breathless even sitting here.
  • Impact: you have stopped your daily walks and you can't do much around the house. It is starting to affect your day-to-day activities: showering and dressing leave you puffed, but you still manage them yourself.
  • Lying flat: you are breathless lying flat. You now sleep on 3 pillows. You used to sleep on 1.
  • At night: for the last 2 nights you have woken up breathless and had to sit on the edge of the bed to get your breath.

Heart (only if asked)

  • Ankles: yes, both ankles are swollen, worse over the last few days. Your shoes feel tight and your socks leave marks.
  • No chest pain, tightness or pressure.
  • No palpitations. You don't usually feel your AF, and nothing has changed.
  • No fainting, blackouts or dizziness.

Lungs (only if asked)

  • A slight dry cough at night when you lie down. No phlegm. No pink frothy spit. No blood.
  • No wheeze that you have noticed. You tried your Ventolin twice and it did not help.
  • No cold, sore throat, runny nose or flu symptoms. No sick contacts.
  • You have never smoked. You worked in a bank all your life: no dust, asbestos or chemical exposure.

General (only if asked)

  • More tired than usual.
  • No fever, sweats or shivers.
  • No weight loss. If anything your trousers feel tighter around the waist. You don't weigh yourself regularly; you think you are usually about 88 kg.
  • Appetite is fine. No nausea or vomiting.

Blood (only if asked)

  • You don't feel pale. No bleeding: no black or bloody stools, no blood in the urine, no nosebleeds, no vomiting blood.

Clots (only if asked): no pain or swelling in one calf more than the other. No long trips, operations or time laid up in bed.

Past medical history

  • Gout.
  • High blood pressure.
  • High cholesterol.
  • Asthma, mild, since you were young.
  • Atrial fibrillation.
  • Heart failure. You see a heart specialist once a year.

Medications

  • Allopurinol.
  • Candesartan.
  • Rosuvastatin.
  • Salbutamol (Ventolin) when needed.
  • Rivaroxaban.
  • Metoprolol.
  • Furosemide.
  • You are not sure of the doses: "My wife sorts them out, and the chemist has the list." You have been taking them all as usual and have not missed any. No dose changes recently.
  • If the candidate asks to check his doses (pharmacy, My Health Record, or phoning his wife), the nurse reads out: furosemide 40 mg each morning, candesartan 16 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 47.5 mg daily, rivaroxaban 20 mg daily, allopurinol 300 mg daily, rosuvastatin 10 mg daily.
  • Only if the candidate asks about any new or over-the-counter medicines, or what you took for your gout: "About 10 days ago my big toe flared up with gout. I bought some Nurofen from the chemist and took 2 tablets three times a day for about 5 days. It settled, so I stopped." You did not see your GP about it.

Diet and fluids (only if asked): no change. You try to keep the salt down and you have not been drinking more than usual.

Allergies: penicillin, which gave you a rash.

Family history

  • Father died of a stroke at 80. He had diabetes and high blood pressure.
  • Mother died of a heart attack at 86. She had heart disease and diabetes.

Social history

  • You live with your wife.
  • Independent with all your daily activities.
  • Three children who live nearby and visit often.
  • Alcohol: 1 or 2 standard drinks at special events only.
  • Non-smoker. No recreational drugs.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: "I think it might be my heart failure, but I don't know." You are worried your heart is getting worse. You miss your walks and want to get back to them. You expect they might "top up the water tablets", and you are hoping you won't have to stay in, but you will if you need to.

If the candidate asks whether anything else is worrying you, say: "Is my heart getting worse?"

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: sitting up at 45 degrees, mildly breathless at rest, speaking in sentences with pauses. Not cyanosed, not pale, not sweaty. Weight on the ED scales today 92 kg.
  • Vital signs: as the nurse reported.
  • Hands: warm, capillary refill 2 seconds. No clubbing. No tophi.
  • Pulse: about 104 to 108/min, irregularly irregular, normal volume.
  • Blood pressure: 144/86.
  • JVP: raised, 5 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees. Hepatojugular reflux positive.
  • Praecordium: apex beat displaced to the 6th intercostal space, anterior axillary line. No heaves or thrills.
  • Heart sounds: first heart sound of variable intensity, second heart sound normal. No murmurs, no added sounds, no rub.
  • Respiratory: trachea central. Expansion slightly reduced at both bases. Dull to percussion at both bases (lowest few centimetres), resonant above. Fine inspiratory crackles at both bases up to about the lower third of each lung. No wheeze. No bronchial breathing.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender. Liver edge just palpable, smooth, non-tender. No ascites.
  • Legs: pitting oedema on both legs to the mid-shins, symmetrical. Mild sacral oedema. Calves soft and non-tender.
  • Right big toe: no redness, warmth or swelling now.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Bernard's identity and asks whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.

Acts on the nurse's observations before finishing the history: keeps Bernard sitting upright, does not lie him flat, and asks for oxygen with a stated target (92 to 96%). Keeps questions focused because he is breathless.
check.d: Credit when he is kept upright and oxygen is requested with a target.

check.x: History
Characterises the breathlessness:
check.d: Credit when the onset and the change in exercise tolerance are both elicited.

kids.x: Onset: gradual over 3 days, getting worse; not sudden
Exercise tolerance: from a couple of kilometres a day to struggling to walk down the block
Impact: stopped daily walks, can't do much around the house, starting to affect ADLs

check.x: Asks about orthopnoea and PND: now sleeps on 3 pillows (used to be 1), breathless lying flat, and has woken breathless on the last 2 nights.
Takes a systems review:
check.d: Source marking: credit when at least 3 systems are covered with relevant questions.

kids.x: Cardiac: chest pain, palpitations and syncope (absent); bilateral ankle swelling (present)
Respiratory: cough, wheeze, pink frothy sputum, URTI symptoms, smoking and occupational exposure (only a dry night cough; salbutamol did not help; never smoked)
Constitutional: fever, fatigue, weight change, appetite, nausea (more tired, trousers tighter, no fever)
Haematological: anaemia symptoms and blood loss, relevant because he is on rivaroxaban (none)

check.x: Asks about precipitants of decompensation:
check.d: Source marking: full marks need the triggers for decompensation as well as 3 systems.

kids.x: Adherence to medicines and to salt and fluid restriction (all taken as usual, no change in diet or fluids)
New or over-the-counter medicines: elicits ibuprofen 2 tablets three times a day for 5 days for a gout flare 10 days ago

check.x: Takes the past medical history: gout, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, asthma, atrial fibrillation and heart failure.
check.d: Credit when heart failure and AF are elicited plus at least 2 others.

check.x: Takes the medication history: allopurinol, candesartan, rosuvastatin, salbutamol PRN, rivaroxaban, metoprolol and furosemide; notes he is unsure of the doses, has taken them all as usual, is already on a diuretic and is anticoagulated.
check.d: Credit when at least 5 of the 7 are named, including furosemide and rivaroxaban, with adherence checked.

check.x: Asks about allergies and the reaction: penicillin, rash.
Takes a family history: father died of a stroke at 80 (diabetes, hypertension), mother died of a heart attack at 86 (IHD, diabetes).
Takes a social history: lives with his wife, independent with ADLs, 3 children nearby who visit often, 1 to 2 standard drinks at special events, non-smoker, no recreational drugs.
check.d: Credit when at least 4 are covered, including smoking.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it might be his heart failure, worried his heart is getting worse, wants to get back to his walks, hopes not to stay in.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs: posture, work of breathing, speech, cyanosis, the nurse's observations, and asks for his weight today (92 kg, about 4 kg above his usual).
Cardiovascular examination for congestion:
check.d: Credit when the pulse and the JVP are examined plus one other.

kids.x: Pulse irregularly irregular at about 104 to 108/min (AF); BP 144/86; warm peripheries
JVP raised 5 cm with positive hepatojugular reflux
Apex displaced to the 6th intercostal space, anterior axillary line
Heart sounds: no murmur, added sound or rub

check.x: Respiratory examination: fine bibasal inspiratory crackles to the lower thirds and dullness at both bases, trachea central, no wheeze.
Examines for peripheral oedema: bilateral pitting oedema to the mid-shins, sacral oedema, soft non-tender calves.
Interpretation
Interprets the observations: RR 24 to 26 and SpO2 91% on room air are in the yellow zone, needing a clinical review; HR white but irregular; BP and temperature normal (afebrile, not shocked).
Interprets the ECG as atrial fibrillation at about 100/min with a narrow QRS and no acute ischaemic change, unchanged from the old ECG apart from the faster rate.
Interprets the NT-proBNP of 4800 ng/L (previously 1350) as supporting acute decompensated heart failure, and the normal hs-troponin as no evidence of myocardial injury.
Identifies an acute kidney injury (creatinine 132 from a baseline of 86, urea 12.4) and links it to the ibuprofen taken with furosemide and candesartan.
check.d: Credit 'triple whammy' or an equivalent explanation.

check.x: Interprets the other bloods: normal Hb (no anaemia), normal WCC and CRP (against infection), mild hyponatraemia and normal potassium.
Reads the chest X-ray:
check.d: Credit when the congestion, the effusions and the absence of consolidation are all stated.

kids.x: Upper lobe venous diversion, Kerley B lines and peribronchial cuffing (interstitial oedema)

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as acute decompensated heart failure, most likely precipitated by the NSAID, justified by known heart failure, worsening exertional breathlessness, orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling, weight gain, raised JVP, crackles, the NT-proBNP and the X-ray.
check.d: Credit when at least 4 supporting features are given and the NSAID is named as the trigger.

check.x: Names differentials or alternative triggers with a feature from this patient: pneumonia or infection (no fever, normal WCC and CRP, no consolidation), ACS (no chest pain, normal ECG and troponin), AF with a fast rate (rate only about 100), asthma (no wheeze, salbutamol did not help), PE (anticoagulated, gradual onset).
check.d: Credit when at least 3 are named, each with a patient feature.

check.x: Management
Escalates to the ED registrar or senior ED doctor, with continuous monitoring and regular observations, and keeps him sitting upright.
Gives oxygen because SpO2 is below 92%, titrated to 92 to 96% (TSANZ), by nasal prongs.
IV furosemide 40 to 80 mg now (at least, and up to 2 times, his usual 40 mg oral daily dose), repeated by response, with fluid balance, daily weights and daily UEC and potassium.
check.d: If the dose is not checked, credit an immediate IV dose of 40 mg or more with a plan to confirm and adjust; do not credit delaying the diuretic.

check.x: Reviews his medicines: stops the ibuprofen and advises no further NSAIDs; reviews candesartan with the registrar because of the AKI; continues metoprolol; continues rivaroxaban after checking the creatinine clearance for the dose.
check.d: Stopping the NSAID is required for credit.

check.x: States the escalation if he worsens: IV or sublingual GTN if congestion persists and systolic BP is above about 110 mmHg (most useful if hypertensive), CPAP or NIV for worsening distress or hypoxaemia, and states that morphine is not routinely recommended.
Admits him under general medicine or cardiology; arranges an echocardiogram; considers a fluid restriction (about 1.5 L a day) with a low-salt diet; plans a gout flare plan that avoids NSAIDs.
Safety netting

Answers Bernard's questions in plain words: fluid built up in and around his lungs and legs because his heart could not cope; the Nurofen, even from the chemist, was the likely trigger and also strained his kidneys; for the next gout flare he should see his GP early for a non-NSAID treatment and keep taking allopurinol; return to walking gradually through cardiac rehabilitation. Checks understanding.
Tells Bernard in plain words to call 000 or come to ED if he is breathless at rest or lying flat, wakes up gasping, has chest pain, faints, or his heart races.

Teaches self-management: weigh himself every morning and see his GP if his weight goes up by more than 2 kg over 2 days or the swelling returns; avoid NSAIDs, including those bought at the chemist, and ask the pharmacist before buying any medicine.

Arranges follow-up: GP review within about a week of discharge with repeat UEC, a heart failure nurse or management program, and cardiology review with the echo to optimise his heart failure medicines.
check.d: Credit when GP review with repeat renal function and specialist or heart failure program follow-up are both arranged.

part2.lead: Here are his observations, the ECG the nurse recorded, his blood results and the chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
Ask these only after the examiner reads question 4, one at a time:

  • "Was it the Nurofen? It was only from the chemist."
  • "What do I take next time my gout flares up?"

You are surprised that a chemist medicine could do this, but relieved there is a reason. If the candidate explains clearly, you agree to the plan and ask them to let your wife know. If they use jargon, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Both sets taken on room air before any treatment; the 14:35 set was taken just before you arrived.
handover.model:
• Read: at triage RR 24 and SpO2 91% on room air are in the yellow zone; HR 104 irregular, BP 146/88 and temperature 36.8 °C are white. At 14:35 RR has risen to 26 (yellow), SpO2 stays 91% (yellow), HR 108 irregular (white), BP 144/86.
  • Meaning: tachypnoea and mild hypoxaemia, slightly worse between sets, with a normal BP and no fever: congestion without shock. The irregular rhythm fits his known AF; the rate is only modestly raised.
  • Changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review, here a senior review now. SpO2 is below 92%, so start oxygen titrated to 92 to 96% (TSANZ) and repeat the observations. Any red-zone value calls for a rapid response.

rows.note: Triage: to acute bay, monitor on, ECG done
Repeat set at bedside before medical review

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG of Mr Bernard Hughes, age 67, recorded at 14:25 today (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: ventricular rate about 100/min.
  • Rhythm: atrial fibrillation. Irregularly irregular, no P waves, fine fibrillatory baseline.
  • Axis: normal, about +30°.
  • PR interval: not measurable (AF).
  • QRS duration: 96 ms. No bundle branch block.
  • QTc: 440 ms.
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression. T waves upright apart from aVR.
  • Other: no pathological Q waves. Normal R wave progression. Voltage criteria for LVH not met.
  • Comparison: previous ECG from his cardiology review 8 months ago shows AF at about 74/min, otherwise unchanged.
handover.model:
• Read: atrial fibrillation at about 100/min, normal axis, narrow QRS, no ST or T wave change, no Q waves; unchanged from 8 months ago apart from a faster rate.
  • Meaning: his known AF, not new. The modestly faster rate is more likely a result of the congestion than its cause. No ischaemic change, which with a normal troponin makes ACS an unlikely trigger.
  • Changes: continue metoprolol and rivaroxaban; expect the rate to settle as he is diuresed; review rate control if it does not.

handover.label: Bloods
handover.model:
• Read: Hb, WCC, neutrophils and platelets normal. Sodium 134 (mildly low), potassium 4.9. Urea 12.4 and creatinine 132 (baseline 86), eGFR 49. CRP, albumin and ALT normal. hs-troponin I 21 ng/L, below the male 99th percentile. NT-proBNP 4800 ng/L, well above the age 50 to 75 rule-in level of 900 and much higher than his previous 1350.
  • Meaning: acute decompensated heart failure. An acute kidney injury (creatinine about 1.5 times baseline, KDIGO stage 1 AKI) after 5 days of ibuprofen on top of furosemide and candesartan. No anaemia, infection or myocardial injury to explain the decompensation.
  • Changes: stop NSAIDs; review candesartan; daily UEC and potassium during diuresis; estimate creatinine clearance (about 60 mL/min by Cockcroft-Gault at 92 kg) before confirming his rivaroxaban dose. This is an estimate only, while creatinine is not stable and at a fluid-overloaded weight; recheck the rivaroxaban dose (20 mg daily if CrCl 50 or more, 15 mg if 15 to 49) as renal function settles.

rows.n: acute HF unlikely below 300; age 50-75 rule-in above 900; previous 1350 (8 months ago)

handover.label: Chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA erect view. Mr Bernard Hughes, 67, taken today at 14:50.

Clinical details: 67-year-old man with known heart failure and AF. Three days of worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea, PND and ankle oedema. Bibasal crackles. SpO2 91% on room air. Afebrile.

Findings:

  • Technical: PA erect, adequate inspiration, not rotated, adequate penetration.
  • Heart and mediastinum: the heart is enlarged, cardiothoracic ratio 0.6. Trachea central. Mediastinum not widened.
  • Lungs: upper lobe venous diversion. Septal (Kerley B) lines at both lung bases. Peribronchial cuffing and mild perihilar haziness. No focal consolidation. No mass.
  • Pleura: small bilateral pleural effusions blunting both costophrenic angles. No pneumothorax.
  • Diaphragm: both hemidiaphragms in a normal position.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no acute bony abnormality.
  • Comparison: chest X-ray 8 months ago: heart size similar; the venous congestion, septal lines and effusions are new.

Conclusion: cardiomegaly with pulmonary venous congestion, interstitial oedema and small bilateral pleural effusions, in keeping with cardiac failure. No consolidation.
handover.model:
• Read: PA erect, adequate film. Cardiomegaly (CTR 0.6), upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines and peribronchial cuffing, small bilateral effusions, no consolidation or pneumothorax; congestion and effusions new compared with 8 months ago.
  • Meaning: interstitial pulmonary oedema and effusions on a background of known cardiomegaly: decompensated heart failure, matching the crackles, basal dullness and raised JVP. No pneumonia as a trigger.
  • Changes: treat the congestion with IV diuretic; the effusions should settle with diuresis; no antibiotics are needed.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Bernard Hughes, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Bernard now, here in the emergency department.
Before Bernard goes home after this admission, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, final-year medical student in ED; Bernard Hughes, 67.
  • Situation: acute decompensated heart failure; RR 26 and SpO2 91% on room air (yellow zone), HR 108 in AF, BP 144/86, afebrile.
  • Background: 3 days of worsening breathlessness (from 2 km to down the block), 3-pillow orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling; known HF, AF on rivaroxaban and metoprolol, hypertension, asthma, gout; adherent; ibuprofen for 5 days for gout 10 days ago; penicillin rash.
  • Assessment: JVP raised, bibasal crackles, oedema to mid-shins, 4 kg weight gain; ECG AF at 100, no ischaemia; NT-proBNP 4800 (was 1350); troponin normal; creatinine 132 from a baseline of 86 (AKI); Hb, WCC and CRP normal; CXR congestion, Kerley B lines, small effusions, no consolidation.
  • Recommendation: please review and admit; oxygen started (target 92 to 96%), IV furosemide 40 to 80 mg now (his usual oral dose is 40 mg), ibuprofen stopped.

Acute decompensated heart failure, precipitated by NSAID use, with an AKI: known HF; 3 days of worsening exertional breathlessness, orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling, weight gain; raised JVP, bibasal crackles, oedema; NT-proBNP 4800; CXR congestion and effusions; ibuprofen for 5 days with creatinine 132 from a baseline of 86.

  • Pneumonia or infection as the trigger: against: no fever or sputum, normal WCC and CRP, no consolidation.
  • ACS as the trigger: against: no chest pain, normal ECG and troponin.
  • AF with a fast ventricular rate: for: known AF, rate up from 74; against: only about 100/min.
  • Asthma exacerbation: for: known asthma; against: no wheeze, salbutamol did not help.
  • PE: against: anticoagulated with rivaroxaban, gradual onset, symmetrical oedema.

1. Escalate and support: ED registrar review, continuous monitoring, sit upright; oxygen by nasal prongs because SpO2 is below 92%, titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%.
  2. IV furosemide 40 to 80 mg now (at least, and up to 2 times, his usual 40 mg oral daily dose), repeated by response; fluid balance, daily weights, daily UEC and potassium.
  3. Medicines: stop ibuprofen; review candesartan with the registrar because of the AKI; continue metoprolol; continue rivaroxaban, checking creatinine clearance for the dose.
  4. If he worsens: IV or sublingual GTN if congestion persists and systolic BP is above about 110 mmHg (most useful if hypertensive); CPAP or NIV for worsening distress or hypoxaemia; morphine not routinely recommended.
  5. Disposition: admit under general medicine or cardiology; echocardiogram; consider fluid restriction about 1.5 L a day with a low-salt diet.

• Explanation: fluid built up in his lungs and legs because his heart could not cope; the Nurofen, even from the chemist, was the likely trigger and strained his kidneys. Avoid NSAIDs; ask the pharmacist before buying medicines.
  • Gout flares: see the GP early. Low-dose colchicine (dose reduced for kidney function), or an intra-articular corticosteroid; oral prednisolone only briefly because it also retains fluid; keep taking allopurinol during a flare (eTG Rheumatology).
  • Daily weights: see the GP if up more than 2 kg over 2 days or the swelling returns.
  • Red flags (000 or ED): breathless at rest or lying flat, waking gasping, chest pain, fainting, racing heart.
  • Follow-up: GP within about a week with repeat UEC; heart failure program; cardiology with the echo; gradual return to walking through cardiac rehabilitation.

ddx.dx: Acute decompensated heart failure precipitated by a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, with acute kidney injury
ddx.for: Known heart failure with 3 days of worsening exertional breathlessness, 3-pillow orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling and weight gain, a raised JVP, bibasal crackles, NT-proBNP 4800, congestion on X-ray, and 5 days of ibuprofen with creatinine 132 from a baseline of 86.
Breathlessness with a night cough and bibasal crackles in an older man.
ddx.against: No fever, sputum or URTI symptoms, normal WCC and CRP, and no consolidation on X-ray.

ddx.dx: Acute coronary syndrome precipitating heart failure
ddx.for: Older man with hypertension, dyslipidaemia and a family history of IHD, presenting with heart failure.
ddx.against: No chest pain, no ischaemic change on the ECG and a normal hs-troponin.

ddx.dx: Atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular rate
ddx.for: Known AF, with the ventricular rate up from 74 to about 100 to 108/min.
ddx.against: The rate is only modestly raised and he has had no palpitations; a clear trigger (NSAID) explains the decompensation.

ddx.for: Known asthma and breathlessness with a night cough.
ddx.against: No wheeze, salbutamol did not help, and he has orthopnoea, PND, oedema and a raised JVP.
He is anticoagulated with rivaroxaban, the onset was gradual, the leg swelling is symmetrical with soft calves, and congestion explains the picture.

guide:
In Part 1, the nurse gives the observations at the start. Bernard can talk in sentences but is breathless, and he will not lie flat. Give the ibuprofen history only if the candidate asks about new or over-the-counter medicines, or what he took for the gout; asking "are you taking your tablets?" alone gets only "all as usual". If the candidate asks to check his doses, the nurse reads out the list in the script. Give examination findings only when the candidate says what they examine. If results are asked for in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order. Bernard asks his two questions after question 4 is read.

The source marking for the systems review gives full marks for 3 relevant systems plus asking about the triggers for decompensation (infection, medicine changes, non-adherence to medicines, salt or fluid, ischaemia, arrhythmia, anaemia); items 7 and 8 reflect this.

A high-performing candidate quantifies the fall in exercise tolerance, elicits orthopnoea, PND and ankle swelling, screens several systems and actively looks for a precipitant, finding the ibuprofen. They examine the pulse, JVP, lung bases and legs, and ask for his weight. In Part 2 they link the AKI to the NSAID with furosemide and candesartan, read the X-ray for congestion and the absence of consolidation, dose IV furosemide from his usual oral dose, stop the NSAID and admit him, then teach daily weights and NSAID avoidance.

A borderline candidate takes a generic breathlessness history, accepts "taking them as usual" without asking about other medicines, and misses the AKI or calls the X-ray pneumonia. Lying him flat, delaying the diuretic, giving antibiotics without evidence of infection, or sending him home on the same medicines without stopping NSAIDs is a serious concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute decompensated heart failure

Bernard has known heart failure and AF. Over 3 days his exercise tolerance has fallen from a couple of kilometres to the end of the block, and he now has orthopnoea (3 pillows instead of 1), PND and bilateral ankle swelling, with about 4 kg of weight gain. On examination he has a raised JVP, bibasal crackles, small effusions and pitting oedema. Together with a markedly raised NT-proBNP and congestion on the chest X-ray, this is acute decompensated heart failure. The key clinical tasks are to decide how severe it is and to find the trigger.

Mild or severe?

Severe decompensation (breathless at rest, hypoxaemia, signs of poor perfusion, or failure of oral treatment) needs hospital care with IV diuretics. Mild decompensation can be managed in the community by finding the trigger, increasing the oral diuretic, restricting fluid and salt, monitoring daily weights and arranging early review. Bernard is breathless at rest with SpO2 91% on room air and an AKI, so he needs admission.

Looking for the trigger

  • Medicines: non-adherence, recent dose changes, and drugs that worsen heart failure: NSAIDs, corticosteroids, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and tricyclic antidepressants. Always ask about over-the-counter medicines.
  • Salt and fluid: dietary indiscretion or excess fluid intake.
  • Cardiac: ischaemia or MI, arrhythmia (especially AF with a fast rate), uncontrolled hypertension.
  • Other: infection (including pneumonia), anaemia, hypoxia, AKI and thyroid disease.

Bernard took ibuprofen for 5 days for a gout flare. NSAIDs cause sodium and water retention and blunt the effect of diuretics. Combined with a diuretic and an ARB they also reduce kidney perfusion (the "triple whammy"), which explains his AKI. Gout is common in heart failure because diuretics raise urate, so this trigger is easy to miss.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: RR and SpO2 in the yellow zone call for a clinical review. A normal BP and warm peripheries mean he is congested but not shocked.
  • ECG: his known AF, slightly faster than before, with no ischaemia. Look for ischaemia, a new or fast arrhythmia and LVH.
  • Bloods: NT-proBNP below 300 ng/L makes acute heart failure unlikely; above the age-adjusted cut-off (900 ng/L at 50 to 75 years) supports it, and comparing with a previous value helps. Troponin, FBE (anaemia), CRP and WCC (infection) and UEC look for triggers and set a baseline for diuresis. His creatinine of 132 is about 1.5 times his baseline of 86, KDIGO stage 1 AKI, presumed to have arisen since the ibuprofen 10 days ago.
  • Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, peribronchial cuffing and effusions show congestion; the absence of consolidation argues against pneumonia.

Management (NHFA/CSANZ 2018, eTG)

  1. Stabilise first, then investigate: sit upright, monitor, and escalate.
  2. Oxygen only for hypoxaemia: TSANZ starts it when SpO2 is below 92% and titrates to 92 to 96%. Bernard's SpO2 of 91% on room air meets this; he has asthma, not COPD, so no lower target is needed.
  3. IV loop diuretic is first-line for congestion. In a patient already on oral furosemide, the IV dose should be at least the usual daily oral dose (up to 2 times it), then adjusted to the response. Bernard's pharmacy list shows furosemide 40 mg each morning, so 40 to 80 mg IV now is appropriate; do not delay the first dose while doses are confirmed. Monitor urine output, fluid balance, daily weights, renal function and potassium.
  4. The old mnemonic LMNOP (Lasix, Morphine, Nitrates, Oxygen, Position) is still taught, but morphine is no longer routinely recommended, oxygen is for hypoxaemia only, and IV or sublingual GTN is considered if congestion persists and systolic BP is above about 110 mmHg (most useful if hypertensive). CPAP or NIV is used for worsening distress or hypoxaemia.
  5. Medicines: stop NSAIDs. Review the ARB while the AKI recovers. Continue the beta-blocker unless he is shocked or bradycardic. Continue the anticoagulant, checking the dose against creatinine clearance.
  6. Admit under general medicine or cardiology, with a repeat echocardiogram to reassess LV function and valves. A fluid restriction (about 1.5 L a day) can be considered while he is congested.

Chronic heart failure care

Once he is stable, his long-term treatment depends on the ejection fraction. For heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, the 2018 guideline sets out an ACE inhibitor or ARB (or an ARNI), a beta-blocker and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, titrated to target doses; newer evidence adds an SGLT2 inhibitor. He needs multidisciplinary care: cardiology, a heart failure nurse or management program, his GP, physiotherapy or cardiac rehabilitation, and a pharmacist review.

Safety netting and follow-up

Before discharge Bernard should know to call 000 or come to ED if he is breathless at rest or lying flat, wakes gasping, has chest pain, faints or has a racing heart. He should weigh himself each morning and see his GP if his weight rises by more than 2 kg over 2 days. He must avoid NSAIDs, including those bought at the chemist, and needs a gout flare plan from his GP that avoids them. Arrange a GP review within about a week with repeat UEC, a heart failure program, cardiology follow-up with the echo, and a gradual return to walking.
points: Orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling and falling exercise tolerance in someone with known heart failure mean decompensation: quantify the change (pillows, distance walked, weight).

Every decompensation has a trigger to look for: non-adherence, salt or fluid, new medicines (NSAIDs, corticosteroids, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers), ischaemia, arrhythmia, infection, anaemia and AKI. Ask specifically about over-the-counter medicines.
An NSAID with a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor or ARB (the 'triple whammy') causes fluid retention and AKI; gout is common in heart failure, so this trigger is easy to miss.
Decide mild or severe: breathlessness at rest, hypoxaemia or AKI needs admission and an IV loop diuretic at least equal to the usual oral daily dose, with daily weights and renal monitoring.
Oxygen only for hypoxaemia (target 92 to 96%), CPAP or NIV for worsening distress, and morphine is no longer routinely recommended.

Safety-net with daily weights (more than 2 kg over 2 days: see the GP), NSAID avoidance, 000 for breathlessness at rest or chest pain, and follow-up with the GP, a heart failure program and cardiology.
